How many of you have a deployment story ready for your next interview, or are you still at the prototype stage?

I have seen this pattern before with mobile, cloud, and SaaS. During every major technology shift, industry debates often center around macro disruption, while the real window to build sustainable value quietly opens and closes.

Recently, S&P Global published a comprehensive report analyzing AI adoption and labor dynamics. The data provides a grounded look at where enterprise AI actually stands today. 

Here are a few key takeaways from the numbers: 
• Productivity gains remain the primary driver: 59% of enterprises prioritize employee productivity, while process efficiency stands at 64%. 
• Headcount reduction is rarely the main goal: Only 24% of organizations cite workforce reduction as a primary objective. 
• The net employment impact is subtle: The global forecast shows a modest net impact of -2 percentage points for the coming year, driven more by changing hiring velocity and task reallocation than outright displacement. 

The report also reveals a clear split based on organization size: 
• Large Enterprises (-13 net impact): Larger organizations are actively restructuring around formal AI strategies and dedicated teams. 
• Small & Medium Businesses (+2 to +3 net impact): Smaller teams are using AI tools as leverage to expand their output and capacity without needing massive headcount additions. 

However, the metric that every AI engineer and Product Manager should pay closest attention to is this:

Only 37% of AI initiatives launched in the past year are currently live and delivering value. Furthermore, only 46% are on track to achieve positive ROI within 12 months. 

Many projects encounter deployment bottlenecks—ranging from data privacy and accuracy concerns to acute technical skill shortages in AI development, software engineering, and governance.

This gap between capital investment and deployed value is currently the single largest opportunity in technology. Organizations do not just need more models or experiments; they need builders and leaders who can systematically design, evaluate, and ship production-grade AI systems that solve real business problems. 

The opportunity to close this gap is open right now.

Are you currently focused on moving AI projects into production and driving ROI, or are you still working through early-stage evaluation? I would love to read your perspective in the comments.

(Link to full S&P Global report in comments)

Here's what I see with data engineers using Claude Code: they build pipelines without specs.

You get a dataset. You write ingestion code. Then cleaning code. Then transformation code. Then analytics. Then a dashboard.

Each step built in isolation.

One change upstream breaks everything downstream.

Example:
- Cleaning script assumes 5 columns
- But raw data has 6 columns
- Pipeline fails silently
- Dashboard shows wrong numbers
- Nobody knows for 3 days

This is fragile.

The problem: No pipeline specification.

Without a spec, you're building blind:
- Each engineer implements cleaning differently
- Transformations are undocumented
- Dashboard metrics are inconsistent
- When data changes, everything breaks

Here's what changes everything:

Spec your entire pipeline upfront.

One document that defines:
- Ingestion: What data comes in? What format? How often?
- Cleaning: How do you handle nulls? Duplicates? Type conversion?
- Transformation: What joins happen? What aggregations? What's the business logic?
- Analytics: What metrics matter? How are they calculated?
- Dashboard: What visualizations? What filters? What refresh rate?

Now when you brief Claude Code, you're not hoping.

Session 1: "Build ingestion following this spec" → Robust ingestion with schema validation
Session 2: "Build cleaning following this spec" → Reproducible cleaning logic with error handling
Session 3: "Build transformations following this spec" → Documented business logic
Session 4: "Build dashboard following this spec" → Metrics in sync with data

Why this matters:

Fragile pipelines:
- Break in production
- Take hours to debug
- Nobody understands how they work
- Can't onboard new engineers

Spec-driven pipelines:
- Work reliably
- Document themselves
- Everyone understands the flow
- Easy to maintain

Stop building fragile pipelines. Start specifying them.

I'm teaching this Friday.

Vibe coding was the move in early 2025. Now it's table stakes.

I told everyone to learn it. It was essential. Still is. But the expectations shifted.

Here's what I'm seeing on the ground: Companies shipped vibe-coded apps. They looked amazing in demos. Then they hit production. No authentication. No telemetry. No way to track KPIs. Fake data everywhere. The speed of build didn't equal quality of output.
The new trend? How do we actually bring the benefits of AI into real production systems?

Vibe coding gets you 80% of the way. The last 20% is where most PMs get stuck. That's the gap we're filling.

Spec-based development is the answer. It's not vibe coding vs production. It's vibe coding + design + specs + code that actually ships.

Instead of PRD → Prompt → App, it's PRD → Engineering Design → Spec → Code → Deploy. Each step adds context. Less hallucination. More production-ready output.

I'm building this into a complete system. Data pipelines, cloud code architecture, observability, the whole stack. Starting tomorrow.

If you're building with Claude Code or v0 and wondering why speed gains aren't materializing, this is for you.

Join the session. Learn spec-based development. Ship production systems.
